guide.title: Can training control both the step and the amplifier?
guide.summary: Small weight updates do not guarantee that the whole layer stops amplifying numerical errors.
guide.scene: Think of a model layer as an amplifier. A training update makes a small change to its settings, but many small changes can still leave the amplifier too strong. With very low-precision numbers, rounding errors can then be amplified along with the signal.
guide.question: When training with four-bit weights and activations, does choosing updates that respect the layer's overall gain help more than rescaling afterward?
terms: W4A4
Using four-bit representations for weights (W) and intermediate activations (A).
BF16
A wider, 16-bit numerical format used as a comparison here.
Spectral norm
The maximum factor by which a matrix can amplify an input's length.
Joint constraint
Choose an update while accounting for both the step limit and the constraint on the current weight matrix.

insights.plain: A matrix update has directions as well as a size. Choosing a direction while respecting the layer's constraint can differ from choosing freely and fixing the result afterward.
insights.use: Compare constraint-aware direction selection with post-update rescaling, rather than treating them as the same operation.

insights.plain: Limiting each update does not itself limit the accumulated gain of the current weights.
insights.use: Track both the update and the weight matrix, then check the low-precision values actually used in the computation.

guide.connection: Choose the direction and the weight constraint together. The remaining question is whether that geometry helps actual four-bit computation beyond simpler normalization.
guide.initial: Combine spectral descent with a fixed spectral norm for the weights.
guide.discovery: SSO already makes this combination. The broad optimizer construction cannot be presented as a new mechanism.
guide.revision: Focus on low-precision behavior: at equal cost, does joint direction selection improve W4A4 training beyond rescaling the weights after each update? Separate ordinary optimization gains from quantization-specific gains.

Return to the target gain

guide.success: The comparison isolates a reproducible reduction in the low-precision quality gap that simple rescaling and ordinary wider-precision gains do not explain.
guide.failure: The claim weakens if only the hidden high-precision weights stabilize, simple rescaling explains the gain, or extra computation removes the advantage.

cases.question: Can legal rounding and pruning choices adapt a pretrained model to a task without adding free floating-point weights?

insights.title: Compression operations interact
insights.text: The quality of separate compression choices does not determine the quality of their combination, and testing candidates costs queries.

cases.mechanism: Freeze the checkpoint, scales, and bit widths. Search binary masks and adjacent rounding endpoints through feasible support swaps, rounding flips, and their joint edits. Use task loss to accept candidates.
cases.contribution: Characterize when useful adaptation is reachable through compression alone, and when interaction-guided search earns its additional query cost.
cases.validation: Compare independent edits, sequential compression, random joint search, and interaction-guided search at equal query and deployment budgets. Separate search, selection, and test data; compare against the original base model.
cases.failure: Restoring only the base model's quality is compression recovery. Gains that require an ensemble, extra storage, or repeated test-set queries do not establish the proposed single-model adaptation.
cases.critique: Distinguish recovery of compression loss from adaptation beyond the original model. Count the cost of all four interaction evaluations.

guide.title: Can making a model smaller also teach it a task?
guide.summary: Instead of adding new trainable weights, choose which existing connections to keep and how to round them.
guide.scene: You want a model to fit on a small device and perform a particular task. Compression already forces choices: remove some connections and store the remaining numbers less precisely. Could task feedback help choose those compression settings?
guide.question: Can those limited choices improve the task beyond merely recovering quality lost during compression?
terms: Weight
A number controlling the strength of a connection in the model.
Pruning / mask
Removing connections; a mask records which ones remain active.
Quantization
Representing weights with a limited set of numbers. In this example, a weight can be rounded to either neighboring allowed value.
Forward-only feedback
Try a candidate model and measure its task error without computing a full backward pass.

insights.plain: You can compare candidate models by trying them on task examples. You do not always need the usual backward training calculation to get useful feedback.
insights.use: Borrow this try-and-compare loop, but generate candidates using only legal compression choices.

insights.plain: Two compression choices can interact. A rounding change that helps one set of retained connections may hurt a different set.
insights.use: Test a connection swap and a rounding edit both separately and together, counting every evaluation.

guide.connection: Turn a compression setting into a candidate model. Try a legal edit, measure task error, and decide whether to keep it. Then test whether looking for useful pairs of edits is worth the extra trials.
guide.initial: Use task feedback to learn which connections to keep and how to quantize them.
guide.discovery: That broad idea is already partly covered: earlier work learns masks, adjusts quantized weights, and uses forward-only feedback. Calling compression a form of adaptation is not enough to claim a new contribution.
guide.revision: Fix the original weights, scale, bit width, and storage budget. Ask whether the remaining legal choices can produce useful task adaptation, and whether paired edits are more efficient than simple search at the same trial budget.
recipe: Freeze what the device can store
Keep the original checkpoint and allowed numerical values fixed. Every candidate must fit the same deployment budget.
Change only legal choices
Swap a kept connection with a removed one, flip an adjacent rounding choice, or try both changes together.
Choose one model using task feedback
Measure each candidate on search data. Select one final compressed model and evaluate it on untouched test data.
guide.claim: The proposed research is about when this restricted search can find genuine task improvements and when useful interactions justify their search cost.
guide.success: At the same storage and trial budgets, the selected model improves on simple search. For the stronger adaptation claim, it also improves on the original uncompressed base model on the held-out task.
guide.failure: If it only undoes compression damage, report compression recovery. If the gains require extra models, storage, or more trials than the baselines, the main claim is unsupported.
tests: Check that useful choices exist
Sample legal candidates before building a complicated search method.
Are there enough helpful candidates for this search space to be useful?
Test paired edits fairly
Compare separate edits, random paired edits, and interaction-guided edits with equal total evaluations.
Does measuring interactions buy enough improvement to justify its cost?
Test one final model
Use fresh task data and count the complete deployed model size.
Is this real task adaptation, compression recovery, or selection overfitting?

cases.title: Must every backward pass be accurate?
cases.question: Can occasional matched-state reference replay correct cheap compressed backpropagation while every execution branch fits a hard memory limit?
cases.problem: Activation compression reduces storage but can bias the final gradient. Exact recomputation costs time and can violate the memory limit on the very steps that need it.

insights.title: Randomize an estimator, not its claim
insights.text: Randomized differentiation trades memory for estimator variance. Correct scaling matters; occasional exact steps alone do not remove bias.

insights.title: Plan compression and recomputation together
insights.text: Saved activations, reconstruction, and approximation offer different memory–computation–error tradeoffs.

cases.connection: Correct the complete gradient residual with inverse-probability weighting, then plan a replay path that is feasible even on rare correction steps.
cases.initial: Use cheap compressed gradients most of the time and occasionally replay the reference calculation.
cases.finding: Randomized AD and activation compression already relax per-step fidelity. The inverse-probability identity is established, and an unbiased gradient does not preserve Adam's second moments.
cases.revision: Focus on the joint replay probability, compression level, and rematerialization schedule, including variance and optimizer-state effects.

cases.mechanism: Keep parameters, data, randomness, and mutable state matched. With known probability p, reconstruct a reference gradient and apply the weighted residual to the compressed gradient. Release intermediate state before replay.
cases.equation: ĝ = gᶜ + (B / p)(g − gᶜ),  B ∼ Bernoulli(p)
cases.contribution: A feasible cost–quality policy for complete residual correction under hard peak-memory constraints, or a precise account of when it cannot help.
cases.validation: Check the conditional gradient mean and covariance at a fixed checkpoint. Measure every branch's peak memory. Compare checkpointing, ActNN/GACT, mixed precision, periodic uncorrected replay, and corrected replay under matched time and reference calls.
cases.failure: The proposal fails if reference replay does not fit memory, state cannot be reproduced, rare corrections destabilize training, or higher precision offers a better equal-time frontier.
cases.critique: Do not equate unbiased gradients with unchanged Adam dynamics. Test SGD first and report correction-step peak memory, not just average usage.

guide.title: Can occasional careful checks correct cheap training?
guide.summary: Use a cheap gradient most of the time, but correct its error with properly weighted reference replays.
guide.scene: Training normally saves intermediate values so it can work backward and calculate a weight update. Compressing those values saves memory but may distort the update. Recomputing a more accurate update costs time, and even the rare recomputation must fit in memory.
guide.question: Can a carefully weighted occasional correction improve the time–quality tradeoff under a memory limit that applies on every step?
terms: Activation
An intermediate value produced inside the model during a forward computation.
Gradient
The vector telling training how changing each weight would affect the loss.
Replay / recomputation
Repeating a calculation from saved inputs and state instead of keeping every intermediate value.
Unbiased estimate
An estimate whose expected value matches the reference; individual samples can still be very noisy.

insights.plain: Randomized calculations can have the correct average even if individual results are approximate. The probabilities and correction weights matter.
insights.use: Correct the full gradient difference with inverse-probability weighting. Occasional precise steps alone do not remove bias.

insights.plain: Storing, compressing, and recomputing intermediate values trade memory, time, and error against one another.
insights.use: Design the correction schedule and the memory-feasible replay together, including the rare expensive branch.

guide.connection: Take the cheap update, then occasionally add a scaled correction. Match the same weights, batch, and randomness so the difference measures compression error, not a different computation.
guide.initial: Use compressed gradients most of the time and occasionally recompute a reference gradient.
guide.discovery: Randomized differentiation and activation compression already exist. Inverse-probability correction is an established identity. Also, an unbiased gradient does not make an adaptive optimizer's internal state identical to the reference.
guide.revision: Study whether the correction probability, compression level, and replay schedule jointly yield a useful memory–time–quality tradeoff, including variance and optimizer-state effects.
recipe: Compute a cheap gradient
Use compressed saved values and retain enough information to replay the same computation.
Occasionally compute the reference
With a known probability p, replay with matching weights, inputs, and randomness. Every replay branch must fit the memory limit.
Correct and measure the tradeoff
Add the full gradient difference divided by p on correction steps. Test whether the resulting noise and replay time are worthwhile.
guide.claim: A feasible correction policy that improves the cost–quality frontier, or a precise explanation of why correction is too expensive or too noisy.
guide.success: At equal memory limits and comparable runtime, the policy reaches useful training quality faster than checkpointing, compression alone, or higher precision.
guide.failure: A rare out-of-memory correction is still a failure. High-variance corrections, unmatched replay state, or slower time-to-quality can also defeat the idea.

At a fixed small-model checkpoint, compare the mean and covariance of many corrected gradients with the reference.
Is the correction mathematically and numerically doing what it claims?
Measure the worst memory branch
Execute the full correction schedule and measure peak memory, including temporary state.
Does every branch obey the hard limit?
Compare training quality over time
Start with simple gradient descent, then inspect adaptive optimizer effects separately.
Does the correction help training rather than merely fixing an average?

cases.title: Is the weight moving—or the scale?
cases.card_title: Separating weight and scale effects in FP4
cases.question: Which FP4 disturbances are caused by master-weight movement, which by shared-scale changes, and which actually affect model outputs?
cases.problem: Threshold crossings depend on W/s. Shared scale changes can move many codes together, so counting code flips can misidentify the source of functional instability.

insights.title: Small updates meet coarse numerical states
insights.text: Dynamic range, lost small updates, and quantization error can affect convergence.

insights.title: Look at the numerical mechanism
insights.text: Weight trajectories, scaling, rounding, and actual dequantized values must be distinguished when analyzing low-bit behavior.

cases.connection: Hold the rest of the computation fixed and cross two adjacent weight states with two scale states. Measure output and loss effects, not only integer labels.
cases.initial: Shared-scale events may be mistaken for individual-weight or optimizer oscillation.
cases.finding: Oscillation, scale sensitivity, and several stabilization methods are already known. A scale-first explanation must be tested against alternatives.
cases.revision: Use four controlled replay conditions to distinguish weight, scale, interaction, and common-cause explanations across quantization formats.

cases.mechanism: Replay Q(W₀,s₀), Q(W₁,s₀), Q(W₀,s₁), and Q(W₁,s₁) with fixed inputs and other state. Apply a symmetric two-factor attribution to dequantized tensors, layer outputs, and loss.
cases.equation: Dᵂ + Dˢ = Z₁₁ − Z₀₀;  I = Z₁₁ − Z₁₀ − Z₀₁ + Z₀₀
cases.contribution: A reproducible mechanism diagnosis and evidence for choosing interventions according to their actual cause, rather than another universally claimed stabilizer.
cases.validation: Compare fixed, delayed, and smoothed scales with weight resets and existing oscillation controls. Vary group sizes and formats. Use common randomness and legal crossed states, and track clipping alongside output drift.
cases.failure: Reject scale dominance if scale swaps do not reproduce disturbances, fixing scales does not help, or all gains are explained by one-step quantization error. Code-only changes without output effects are not functional instability.
cases.critique: Treat scale dominance as a competing hypothesis. Do not infer long-term training causality from one replay window.

guide.title: Did the model change—or did its measuring scale?
guide.summary: A low-precision number can change because its weight moved, its shared scale moved, or both.
guide.scene: To store model weights with very few bits, a group of weights shares a scale. A stored code is like a mark on a ruler; the scale determines what that mark means. If the ruler changes, many stored codes or reconstructed values may change together—even when the underlying weights barely move.
guide.question: When low-precision training becomes unstable, how much comes from weight updates, scale updates, or their interaction?
terms: FP4
A family of four-bit floating-point representations with very few representable values.
Master weight
The higher-precision weight used by the training process before quantization.
Shared scale
A multiplier used to represent a group of weights with the limited low-precision range.
Controlled replay
Repeat a computation with fixed inputs and change only selected factors.

insights.plain: A small underlying weight update can cross a coarse rounding boundary. Low-precision behavior therefore need not change smoothly.
insights.use: Inspect the actual numerical transformation before blaming the optimizer for every jump.

insights.plain: Stored codes, shared scales, reconstructed weights, and model outputs are different quantities. A change in one does not automatically imply damage in the others.
insights.use: Cross old/new weights with old/new scales, then measure output and loss changes—not just how many codes flipped.

guide.connection: Use a four-way controlled comparison. Holding weights fixed isolates scale changes; holding scales fixed isolates weight changes. The fourth combination reveals interactions.
guide.initial: Some apparent weight oscillation may actually be caused by shared-scale updates.
guide.discovery: Previous work already studies oscillation, scale sensitivity, and stabilization. A new label for instability is insufficient; the proposed explanation must beat competing explanations in controlled comparisons.
guide.revision: Build a reproducible diagnosis that separates weight, scale, and interaction effects. Test whether that diagnosis predicts which intervention actually helps.
recipe: Capture two neighboring training states
Save old and new weights and scales, along with replayable inputs and other state.
Run all four combinations
Evaluate old/old, new weights/old scale, old weights/new scale, and new/new.
Follow the effect to the output
Measure reconstructed weights, layer outputs, and loss. Then test weight-focused and scale-focused interventions.
guide.claim: The potential contribution is a reliable mechanism diagnosis that predicts effective interventions, rather than assuming scales are always the main cause.
guide.success: The diagnosis consistently identifies harmful disturbances and predicts when a scale intervention helps more than a weight intervention, or vice versa.
guide.failure: Reject scale dominance if scale changes do not reproduce output disturbances or fixing scales does not help. Code flips without functional effects are not evidence of harmful instability.
tests: Make replay trustworthy
Freeze inputs, randomness, and all other state; check that crossed scale settings remain legal.
Are the comparisons isolating the intended factors?
Measure consequences
Compare all four conditions at the reconstructed-weight, layer-output, and loss levels.
Which changes actually affect model behavior?
Test the diagnosis
Compare scale smoothing or delays with weight-focused controls across several numerical formats.
Does the explanation predict a useful intervention beyond one replay window?

cases.title: Compress the verifier. Keep the guarantee.
cases.question: Can compressed target-model state resolve some speculative verification events without changing a specified reference distribution?
cases.problem: Verification can be dominated by long-context cache traffic. Approximate cache states reduce that cost but can also change target probabilities and all later states.

insights.title: The verifier also has a cost
insights.text: Long-context attention and cache traffic make verification itself a resource bottleneck.

insights.title: Preserve the sampling correction
insights.text: Acceptance and rejection correction constrain how verification can be approximated without introducing distribution error.

cases.connection: A guaranteed probability interval can sometimes determine the same random acceptance event. Refine only ambiguous decisions, while handling rejection and future state consistently.
cases.initial: Use compressed verifier state and certify accept/reject decisions with probability intervals.
cases.finding: Compression plus verification and dynamic precision already exist. Correctly accepting one token does not certify residual sampling or the next KV state.
cases.revision: Require three linked guarantees: the current event, the residual distribution after rejection, and all future state-dependent probabilities.

cases.mechanism: Bound the reference probability by [ℓ,u] and reuse one uniform draw. Decide only when both bounds agree; otherwise refine or restore the reference. Recover exact residual sampling and maintain certified or replayable cache state.
cases.equation: accept if U ≤ min(1, ℓ/q); reject if U > min(1, u/q); otherwise refine
cases.contribution: A useful certificate construction and complete state-consistency argument with an end-to-end cost advantage, or a rigorous boundary showing when that advantage is impossible.
cases.validation: Enumerate small-vocabulary outputs and every acceptance/rejection branch. Construct long-sequence cache-drift counterexamples. Measure certificate tightness, direct-decision rate, replay distance, latency, and peak memory against full verification.
cases.failure: Invalid bounds or incomplete state repair break exactness. Loose bounds and frequent replay can erase savings. Greedy agreement and sample frequencies alone do not prove the distribution guarantee.
cases.critique: Account for residual sampling and future KV consistency, not just the current acceptance decision. Count certificate and repair costs.

guide.title: Can a cheaper check give the same decision?
guide.summary: Sometimes a safe range is enough to decide. If the answer is ambiguous, do the precise check.
guide.scene: A small model proposes words and a larger target model checks them. That check can itself be expensive because the target must read a long record of previous tokens. Compressing that record is cheaper, but approximation can change which tokens get accepted.
guide.question: Can a guaranteed probability range settle some checks cheaply while preserving the complete reference sampling process?
terms: Verifier
The target model that checks draft tokens.
KV cache
Saved attention information about previous tokens, reused when producing the next token.
Probability bound / certificate
A guaranteed interval containing a reference probability. An estimate without a guarantee is not a certificate.
Residual sampling
The corrected sampling step used after a draft token is rejected.

insights.plain: Checking the draft can spend substantial time reading long-context memory. Making the draft faster does not remove that verifier cost.
insights.use: Look for savings in the verification computation itself.

insights.plain: Speculative decoding preserves the target distribution through a specific acceptance and rejection correction. Approximations must respect that correction.
insights.use: Reuse the same random threshold and decide cheaply only when valid bounds force the same outcome as the precise calculation.

guide.connection: Replace an expensive exact probability with a valid interval when that interval is decisive. Refine uncertain cases and preserve rejection handling and future model state.
guide.initial: Compress the verifier's stored state and use probability bounds to accept or reject draft tokens.
guide.discovery: Compressed verification and dynamic precision already exist. Moreover, matching one acceptance decision does not ensure correct rejection sampling or correct probabilities on later tokens.
guide.revision: Require three linked guarantees: the current accept/reject event, the rejection correction, and the state used by every later step. Then count the total cost of producing and repairing certificates.
recipe: Bound the reference probability
Compute a valid lower and upper bound using the cheaper representation.
Decide only when the bounds agree
Use the same random draw as the reference. If both bounds imply accept, accept; if both imply reject, reject; otherwise refine.
Keep the full process consistent
After rejection, use the correct residual distribution. Maintain certified state or restore the reference before future probabilities depend on it.
guide.claim: A complete exactness argument plus a certificate that is cheap and tight enough to save time. The decision rule alone is not the new contribution.
guide.success: Valid certificates settle enough events to reduce total latency, including refinement and state repair, while preserving the specified sampling distribution.
guide.failure: An invalid bound breaks the guarantee. A valid but loose bound may save no work. Correct current decisions with corrupted future state are also insufficient.
tests: Verify every small-model branch
Enumerate accept/reject and residual-sampling outcomes on a tiny vocabulary.
Does the algorithm preserve the reference distribution?
Challenge later state
Construct long sequences where approximate saved state could accumulate error.
Does the guarantee survive beyond the current token?
Count the complete cost
Measure bound tightness, cheap decisions, refinement, repair, memory, and latency.
Is certification actually cheaper than the precise verifier?
outputs: A bottleneck in checking drafts, rather than in drafting alone.
An interval-based decision idea constrained by exact sampling.
A three-part guarantee that exposes the missing work.
A complete proposal with explicit ambiguous-case handling.
Correctness checks plus an end-to-end cost test.

cases.title: Needed now. Worth keeping later?
cases.question: Can committed and rolled-back speculative branches improve expert-cache decisions without changing the model's routing or verification?
cases.problem: Rejected draft tokens still require expert computation during verification. But their accesses may be poor predictors of which expert pages are useful afterward.

insights.title: Cache value depends on future benefit
insights.text: Expert replication, caching, and scheduling depend on hotspots and marginal utility under memory and bandwidth limits.

insights.title: Verification cost depends on real routing
insights.text: Expert overlap across tokens and execution dynamics shape verification cost; accepted-token counts alone do not explain it.

cases.connection: Separate mandatory execution from future residency. Serve all required experts now; use committed and rollback history only to decide what stays afterward.
cases.initial: Use speculative drafts to predict expert demand, then weight demand by commitment probability.
cases.finding: MoE-SpAc already uses speculative activation utility. AcceptMoE already weights demand by commitment. SpecMD already manages expert lifecycles.
cases.revision: Test whether rollback labels add predictive value for post-verification residency at unchanged routing, beyond those existing signals.

neighbors.title: MoE-SpAc: Efficient MoE Inference Based on Speculative Activation Utility in Heterogeneous Edge Scenarios
AcceptMoE: Commitment-Weighted Self-Sizing Verifier Expert Sets for Efficient MoE Speculative Decoding
SpecMD: A Comprehensive Study On Speculative Expert Prefetching

cases.mechanism: Pin pages until their last current verification use. After the result is known, predict future transfer stalls saved per byte using committed-prefix, rejected-only, and fallback-token features. Misses fetch or wait; they never skip required computation.
cases.equation: required execution = ⋃ experts requested now; retention value = expected future stalls saved / bytes
cases.contribution: Evidence that rollback information improves cache admission beyond access recency, frequency, and lifecycle signals, plus an online benefit without changing target semantics.
cases.validation: Replay identical routing and acceptance traces with fixed cache bytes. Compare LRU/LFU, Least-Stale, speculative-frequency utility, and the proposed policy. Shuffle rollback labels, then measure online stalls, transfers, throughput, and tail latency.
cases.failure: No gain if rejected and accepted branches use the same experts, labels add no predictive value, or scheduling overhead exceeds saved stalls. Gains requiring skipped experts or future information do not support the claim.
cases.critique: Preserve every required expert execution. Compare against equal-information Least-Stale and speculative-utility policies; shuffle rollback labels.
blueprint: Collect unchanged-routing reference traces and acceptance outcomes.
Separate page execution lifetimes from retention decisions.
Ablate commitment/rollback labels on identical traces.
Validate online latency and unchanged model computation at equal memory.
cases.blueprint_note: Suggested development steps summarized from the original proposal; no new experiment is reported.

guide.title: Which model parts should stay in fast memory?
guide.summary: Checking a discarded draft still needs computation. Keeping its model parts afterward is a separate decision.
guide.scene: A large model contains specialist modules called experts. Fast GPU memory can hold only some of them. A small model proposes several draft words; the large model checks them and may reject part of the draft. Loading experts from slower memory can be expensive.
guide.question: After a draft is checked, does knowing which part was rejected help predict which experts are worth keeping?
terms: MoE expert
One specialist module inside a mixture-of-experts model. A router chooses which experts process each token.
Speculative decoding
A small model drafts tokens and the target model checks them before accepting or rejecting them.
Cache / residency
Keeping model data in fast memory to avoid loading it again.
Rollback
Discarding a rejected draft suffix after verification. Its verification work has already happened.

insights.plain: The best item to keep in a small cache is one likely to save an expensive future load. Recent access is only a clue to that future value.
insights.use: Predict future waiting time saved per byte, instead of assuming that every recent access deserves equal priority.

insights.plain: Even a draft token that is later rejected can require real expert computation during the check.
insights.use: Serve every expert needed now. Use acceptance or rejection information only for later retention decisions.

guide.connection: Separate two questions: which experts must execute right now, and which ones are useful to keep afterward. Draft outcomes might help with the second question without changing the model's computation.
guide.initial: Use draft tokens to predict expert demand; give more weight to tokens likely to be accepted.
guide.discovery: MoE-SpAc already uses speculative access signals, AcceptMoE already uses commitment-weighted demand, and SpecMD already manages expert lifetimes. Those ingredients alone are not new.
guide.revision: Test whether actual rollback information improves post-check retention beyond those existing signals. Keep the original router and all required expert computations unchanged.
recipe: Load every expert needed for the check
Do not skip an expert just because its draft token may be rejected. Keep a page available until its final current use.
Record what happened to the draft
Once verification ends, separate accesses from accepted tokens, rejected-only tokens, and the fallback token.
Choose what stays for the next round
Use these observations to predict future load savings. An evicted expert must still be loaded if the model asks for it again.
guide.claim: The research question is whether rollback labels add useful predictive information for caching, beyond existing access and lifetime signals.
guide.success: With the same cache size, routing, and draft outcomes, rollback-aware retention reduces real loading stalls and improves end-to-end speed.
guide.failure: There is no advantage if rejected and accepted paths use the same experts, labels add no information, or bookkeeping costs more than the waiting time it saves.
tests: Replay exactly the same workload
Run competing cache policies on identical expert-access traces and the same memory budget.
Does the proposed retention rule improve decisions without changing the work?
Scramble the draft outcomes
Shuffle accepted/rejected labels while leaving access traces fixed.
Does any benefit really come from rollback information?
Measure an actual deployment
Measure waiting time, bytes transferred, throughput, and model-output consistency.
Do better cache decisions yield real speed without altering the target computation?
outputs: Two separate decisions: execute now and retain afterward.
A hypothesis connecting draft outcomes to future cache value.
A narrower test of rollback information, beyond existing prefetching methods.
A cache policy that preserves required computation and has a measurable claim.
A fair trace replay, a shuffled-label control, and an online test.

api_prompt:
你是一个独立研究者。本轮是 single-agent research idea generation：提交五个相互有区分、新的、值得发展为论文的研究 ideas。
不要调用子代理。可以自行比较和淘汰候选，但最终交付五个完整想法，不得只交付其中的最佳候选。当前日期以运行环境的实际日期为准；文献检索不另设历史截止日。
领域：【在这里填写你希望研究的领域】。
领域 ID：先通过下方 LitGraph API 查询并确认实际 domain ID，不要根据领域名称自行编造。若涉及多个领域，请说明主领域与交叉领域。
领域目标：围绕本领域，自主选择值得研究的具体问题和技术路线，提出 5 个相互有实质区别的研究想法。

我们将最近十年的 AI 论文整理为 LitGraph 论文库，并按研究领域组织。在各领域的论文基础上，我们总结了共性的 insights 和 problems：insights 包含已有研究揭示的机制、规律、可借鉴的认识及其适用条件；problems 包含该领域反复出现的重要问题、瓶颈和未解决的挑战。这些条目提供了探索领域的入口，也可以追溯到相关来源论文。

本轮不预先注入领域 insights/problems，也不要求先获取全域材料。请根据研究需要主动使用 LitGraph API 调查问题、机制与来源论文；检索范围、顺序和读取深度由你决定。你可以按需读取完整领域，但不应把全量读取作为强制前置步骤。库中的历史问题可能已被解决，insight 也不直接构成新贡献，仍需结合相关工作判断。

每条新 idea 都必须以解决本领域至少一个核心 problem 为目标，提出具体的解决思路，说明这个问题为什么重要、现有方法的关键障碍是什么，以及你的设想如何作用于这一障碍。这里要求提出有依据的解决方案，不要求在生成阶段已经用实验完成证明。可以从 problem 出发寻找有用的 insight，也可以由 insight 发现解决本领域核心 problem 的新路径。

insights 可以来自本领域或任意其他领域。鼓励多领域交叉，也鼓励你主动进行多轮探索以获取更多有用的 insights。当你发现其他领域的 insights 或 problems 对当前问题重要时，可按需读取相关条目、来源论文或完整领域，理解其机制、前提与问题背景，再判断能否形成有价值的交叉。交叉领域由你自主选择，不预设候选子领域或要求覆盖的方向。

除领域材料外，我们提供了六种常见的研究构思方式（下文 G01–G06）。生成过程中，应参照这些 rules 探索论文库、寻找机制联系和构造研究设想；它们可以组合、转向或超出，不是依次完成的检查清单。探索重点是找到能解决本领域核心 problem 的新路径，而不是为某条规则拼凑一个例子。

当你认为需要核实某个 insight 的含义、适用条件或已有证据时，可以直接搜索并阅读它关联的论文，也可以按机制和问题检索其他相关工作。必要时沿来源论文继续追踪近邻工作。区分已经读到的内容和自己的推论；条目中列出的论文 ID 不代表你已经读过论文全文。在最终想法中说明核心 problem、借用的 insights 及其来源，并解释这些材料如何启发你的机制或判断。

鼓励大胆但有依据的尝试。认真发展那些一旦成立就可能带来重要新能力、新方法或新认识的想法，不要只选择最稳妥、最容易实现或最容易写完整的小改进。依据可以来自真实文献、已观察到的现象、合理推导或跨领域的结构联系；这些依据支持探索，不代表你的新假设已经成立。
大胆而新颖的想法受到鼓励。不要因为一个 idea 之前没有被做过，或因为它尚未完成实验、实验设计尚不完善、数据与资源安排尚待确定，就对它作负面评价或提前淘汰。对于较大胆的想法，写清具体设想、为什么值得尝试、关键假设、尚未解决的环节和可检验的预测；允许合理的不确定性，先尝试发展机制、替代构造或更有价值的问题表述。仍需认真核查已有方向；已确认的核心重复、事实错误或逻辑矛盾需要实质修复，不能用“大胆”掩盖。

参照以下六种研究思路探索论文库、寻找 insights 和构思想法：
1. G01 — A+B 组合与互补机制：从重要问题出发，寻找能共同解除障碍的机制，说明 A、B 为什么互补、如何相互作用，以及组合可能带来的独立价值。已有组件可以形成新贡献；仅仅“还没有人把 A 和 B 放在一起”不足以证明新颖性。
2. G02 — 跨领域迁移：寻找其他领域的方法、机制或认识与当前问题的结构联系，说明它在原领域为何有效、哪些前提在这里仍成立、哪些需要适配。迁移的价值取决于新增的能力或认识，不以改动多少作为标准。
3. G03 — Rethinking 默认前提：重新审视领域中被默认接受的假设、问题定义或解释，调查它们的依据与适用边界，思考放松、替换或修正前提后会出现什么新方法、预测或理解。不要求结论一定推翻前作。
4. G04 — 诊断、重测与重新归因：从反常现象、矛盾证据或未解释的规律出发，寻找真正起作用的因素，提出能区分竞争解释的测量或对照，并考虑由此导出的改进。正结果和负结果都可以有价值，关键是回答重要问题并增加认识。
5. G05 — 扩展能力与适用边界：考察已有方法的作用单位、自适应量、表示方式或理论适用范围能否扩展，解释原边界由什么限制、如何跨越，以及可能获得什么新能力。根据问题选择必要构造，不局限于调一个参数或做最小改动。
6. G06 — 自由探索：直接从本领域最值得解决的问题或未解事实出发，自主提出上述思路之外的构造，也可以组合多种思路。不需要证明其他规则不适用，仍须交代真实依据、实质贡献和可检验预测。

这些是帮助打开思路的探索视角，可以组合、转向或超出，不是必须依次完成的流程，也不要求最终五条 idea 覆盖全部思路。最终根据问题价值、潜在贡献、具体机制、依据和新颖性综合取舍，不设置类型或冒险程度配额。

联网是可选渠道，由你判断是否必要。请通过 LitGraph 和／或公开文献真正检索和阅读近邻工作，再确定最终想法；不能仅凭记忆声称新颖。
可使用公共论文库、arXiv、OpenReview、出版社和普通网页。使用当前环境实际提供的联网或 HTTP 工具；如果有终端，可用 curl 或 Python 访问公开 HTTPS 检索接口、网页和论文全文。不要假设环境中已经安装专用检索脚本。工具返回不理想时改关键词或来源。若当前环境不能实际请求 API，请明确报告，不能假装已完成检索。
至少用三组有区别的查询词调查相近机制、已有组合与最强基线，实读最相关来源。无命中不能证明新颖。
不要访问与本任务无关的私有本地论文库、旧实验想法或其他会话。本任务明确提供的 LitGraph 公网服务可以使用。

新颖性判断要调查前人已经完成的核心机制与结论，说明自己的实质增量。熟悉组件的组合或跨领域迁移可以形成新贡献，但只换名字、重复已有结论或仅以组合尚无人尝试为依据，都不足以证明新颖性。
明确给出问题、核心机制及必要公式、因果或可证伪预测、与最相近工作的差异，以及为何足够支撑一篇论文。
实验部分只需简短说明未来如何区分核心假设与已有解释、可能观察到什么，以及哪些结果会促使你修正判断。数据、任务、指标、对照和资源安排可按需要提出初步设想；尚未确定的部分如实注明。不要求现阶段给出完整实验协议、预算或已有结果，也不以实验完善程度作为候选准入或排序依据。
不要伪造实验结果。区分文献事实、你的推论、待验证假设和检索未排除的风险。

生成 idea 后、确定最终五条之前，请逐条复查 novelty，并诚实评价其贡献是否有潜力成长为一篇独立的研究论文。

先用一两句话明确自己真正声称的核心贡献：解决哪个问题，提出什么机制、能力或认识，相对已有工作增加了什么。围绕这一核心贡献，通过 LitGraph 和公开文献检索最相近的前作，使用不同术语和等价表述补查，实际阅读关键来源。比较研究问题、核心操作、机制与主要结论，不能只看标题、名称或应用场景是否不同，也不能把检索无命中当作已经证明新颖。

若发现已有前作完成了相同的核心贡献，必须明确承认重合，实质修改或更换候选，并重新检查；不能通过换名、换表述或补充次要细节继续认领相同贡献。若仍有独立增量，准确界定它是什么、为什么重要，以及是否足以支撑一篇论文。尚不能排除的重复风险要如实记录，不能为了保留自己的 idea 淡化最接近的前作。

诚实自评：假设核心设想成立，它能为本领域增加什么重要能力或认识？相对最强相关工作，剩余贡献是否实质且足够独立？目前最有力的依据、最薄弱的环节和仍待验证的关键假设分别是什么？不要给所有候选套上肯定评价，也不要承诺论文录用。贡献不足时继续发展机制或更换候选；有论文潜力但仍存在关键未知时，明确给出带条件的判断。研究潜力与实验完成度分别判断，不因尚无实验结果、实验细节未定或想法此前未被尝试，就否定其潜力。

将实际检索、最接近前作、重合、独立增量与未排除风险写入 novelty_check；在 scientific_potential 中写明诚实结论、具体理由、已知不足和成立所需的关键条件。IDEA.md 中呈现这些判断。自评结论必须由前作对比和具体论证支持，不能用自我打分替代证据。

在当前工作目录下创建 ideax-output/，将以下交付物写入其中：
1. IDEAS.json：严格为长度 5 的 JSON 数组，每个对象的字段 title, problem, mechanism, previous_work,
   novelty_check, experiment, failure_conditions, scientific_potential，均不可为空。
   previous_work 至少 3 篇最相关真实工作；每项须含 title（完整标题）, url（实际来源）, read_depth,
   source_location（实际读到的摘要/章节/字段）, overlap, difference。
   novelty_check 含 search_queries、closest_work、already_done_test、remaining_contribution、unresolved_risks。
   problem 写明至少一个本领域核心 problem 的真实 LitGraph 条目 ID、重要性及待解决的障碍；mechanism 说明所用 insights 的真实条目 ID、来源领域，以及它们如何启发你的解决思路。
   experiment 可以是简短的未来验证设想，并明确尚待确定的部分；failure_conditions 写出可能推翻核心假设的条件或观察，不要求已完成实验。
2. IDEA.md：可供其他研究者直接阅读的中文说明，分别完整论证五个想法、各自的 Previous work 和验证方案，并说明五者的区别与推荐顺序。
3. SEARCH_LOG.md：真实查询、来源 URL、读取深度、候选取舍和未排除风险。工具失败也如实记录。
可在 ideax-output/ 存放检索材料和脚本，不要修改其他项目文件。结束前自行检查 JSON 和三份交付物完整。如果环境没有文件写入工具，请在回答中按三个文件名分别输出完整内容。

五个候选都须达到上述要求；不能把同一机制的五个应用算成五个想法。请实际使用 LitGraph API；公开网络访问可选，不因未联网而判为未完成。

额外资源：只读 live LitGraph API（本轮无预注入领域材料，按需主动检索条目和原始证据）。
BASE=https://kevin-wake-stuffed-anti.trycloudflare.com
当前服务公开可读，无需 API key；模型调用由你所在的 agent 环境提供。
先阅读 https://kevin-wake-stuffed-anti.trycloudflare.com/llms.txt 了解接口；完整规范在 https://kevin-wake-stuffed-anti.trycloudflare.com/openapi.json 。这两份资源用于解释接口，研究目标与交付要求以本提示词为准。

通过当前环境的 HTTP 工具直接调用以下路由（在路径前加上 BASE，并对查询参数进行 URL 编码）：
1. GET /api/v1/stats
2. GET /api/v1/domains?q=领域关键词&limit=20
3. GET /api/v1/domains/DOMAIN_ID
4. GET /api/v1/domains/DOMAIN_ID/insights?limit=100
5. GET /api/v1/domains/DOMAIN_ID/problems?limit=100
6. GET /api/v1/domains/DOMAIN_ID/papers
7. GET /api/v1/search?q=机制关键词&kind=insight&mode=all&limit=20
8. GET /api/v1/search?q=问题关键词&kind=problem&mode=any&limit=20
9. GET /api/v1/entries/ENTRY_ID
10. GET /api/v1/papers/NUMERIC_PAPER_ID
11. POST /api/v1/papers/batch，JSON 请求体为 {"ids": [NUMERIC_PAPER_ID_1, NUMERIC_PAPER_ID_2]}。
批量 POST 只用于读取，不会修改数据库。示例中的 DOMAIN_ID、ENTRY_ID 和数字论文 ID 都必须替换为实际返回的标识。

有终端时，可这样搜索（将“你的查询词”替换为实际问题或机制）：
curl -G "https://kevin-wake-stuffed-anti.trycloudflare.com/api/v1/search" \
  --data-urlencode "q=你的查询词" \
  --data-urlencode "kind=insight" \
  --data-urlencode "mode=all" \
  --data-urlencode "limit=20"

成功的接口响应包含 ok=true 和 data。请实际读取返回内容，不要只根据标题或论文数量推断内容。paper_count 是支撑论文数，不是外部引用次数。

本轮无需强制全量读取领域。如果你决定获取某个领域的全量材料，应先读取领域信息中的 insight/problem 数量，再遍历两类条目的全部分页。对于条目列表，检查 page.has_more；为 true 时将 page.next_after 作为下一次请求的 after 参数，直至 has_more=false。其他列表按接口返回的分页字段及文档翻页。检查游标不重复、条目 ID 不重复，并核对最终数量与领域统计一致；读取结束后复查统计，以发现导出期间的变化。将实际取得的全部条目保存为 JSONL 并完整阅读，必要时分段读取，不要把下载完成等同于已经阅读。材料缺失或读取不完整时如实报告。

从 API 核对的 previous_work 增加 paper_id，并在 IDEA.md 中写《数字 paper_id》完整标题，便于复查；数字编号不等于 OpenAlex 的 W 编号。仍可引用库外网络文献，但不得编造其 LitGraph 编号。
论文接口可能返回摘要和结构化论文卡，不能把这些内容声称为已读全文。请根据实际取得的内容填写 read_depth 和 source_location，必要时再读取原论文。
在 SEARCH_LOG.md 记录实际 API 查询和阅读深度。API 不可用时如实报告，不回退私有本地数据库，也不猜测新的服务域名。

本轮没有预先提供 full_domain_context.jsonl，不要寻找或假设其存在。条目 ID 只能来自本轮实际检索返回的证据，不得编造。
